title: Why copying #1 is a trap: luck, survivorship and tournament effects in business
summary: Jason Cohen argues that markets work like single-elimination tournaments, so the "undefeated" winner proves less about repeatable skill than we assume. He urges skepticism toward "be more like Google/Apple/37signals" advice, learning from companies at every rank, and striving to become a better version of yourself rather than a clone of #1.

principles.text: The market is a tournament that always yields one winner, so #1's success may not come from a repeatable, codifiable law.
principles.quote: I'm not sure we can assume the contest (marketing, sales, product) and tournament (the marketplace) picks #1 based on a repeatable, codify-able law.

principles.text: Don't assume the top company is the rightful leader; skill and luck are mixed in unknown proportions.
principles.quote: We tend to fixate on whoever is #1, in business as with sports, tacitly assuming that the contest is mostly skill and therefore the tournament has selected the rightful leader.

principles.text: Lessons exist well below the top ranks; smaller successes can teach as much as the giants.
principles.quote: Isn't the #4253 largest company in the world still a success story, perhaps with new lessons and perspectives?

principles.text: When told to 'be more like Google', question whether the advisor simply has no other reference point.
principles.quote: When someone insists you need to be "more like Google," consider that perhaps it's the only thing they know to compare to.

principles.text: Celebrity-company playbooks rarely fit a young startup; most successful companies don't resemble them.
principles.quote: When someone insists you need to be "more like 37signals," consider that almost no successful companies are like 37signals.

principles.text: Aim to become a better version of what you already are, not a copy of the market leader.
principles.quote: It's fine to muse about being #1, but let's not all strive to become just like #1.
